metadataDescription: From the planets to the edge of the observable universe in one zoom, where distance is also how long the light has been on its way.
canvasLabel: Interactive map from the planets to the observable universe

camera.body: Drag to turn, scroll or pinch to zoom.

guide.title: Guide
guide.body: Learn how far the universe reaches, step by step.

experiences.title: Viewing modes
experiences.body: Immersive: just the view, no controls. Drift: sit back while the camera flies itself to the music.

viewHints.heliosphere: Five probes on their way out, and the edge of the Sun's wind they crossed.
viewHints.stars: Proxima, Alpha Centauri and Barnard's Star in their real directions. The ring is Proxima's distance; the sky behind is the real one.
viewHints.galaxy: Our galaxy, about {galaxyLy} light-years across. The gold line is the Sun's path.
viewHints.observable-universe: Everything light has had time to reach us from. The microwave background is the farthest light we can see.

methods.radar: Measured by radar and spacecraft tracking
methods.tracking: Measured by radio tracking of the probes
methods.orbits: From orbits fitted to tracked positions
methods.parallax: Measured by parallax: the shift as Earth circles the Sun
methods.galacticCentre: From parallax and stars orbiting the central black hole
methods.candles: From Cepheids and red giants of known brightness

sun.title: The Sun in the Galaxy
sun.speed: About {value} km/s circular speed here; the Sun itself moves ~{sun} km/s
sun.radial: Out to ~{value} farther and back, every ~{period} million years
sun.vertical: ±{value} over ~{period} million years; now ~{height} north, climbing
sun.body: We sit at the inner edge of the Local Arm (the Orion Spur), between the Sagittarius–Carina and Perseus arms, neither at the centre nor at the rim. Since it formed the Sun has lapped the Galaxy about {laps} times, clockwise seen from the north galactic pole. The gold line is its path over the last two laps, a schematic: its true angle that long ago is not known.
sun.caution: The wobble amplitudes are typical values from stellar-dynamics estimates; studies differ. A star's galactic path is not a closed ellipse.

bulge.title: Bulge and bar
bulge.bar: About {value} end to end, estimates {range}; ~{angle}° to the Sun–centre line
bulge.body: The Milky Way is a barred spiral. The centre is a boxy, peanut-shaped bulge of old stars, X-shaped seen edge-on, inside a longer, thinner bar whose ends feed the spiral arms. At the very middle sits Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about {mass} Suns. The point density is a sketch, not a star catalogue.
bulge.caution: Do not measure the bar's length off this drawing.

halo.title: Dark-matter halo
halo.body: The pale overlay projects an inferred NFW density profile constrained by the 2026 Gaia Cepheid analysis. It becomes denser toward the centre and fades outward. The optional circle marks a density convention; the model continues beyond it.
halo.caution: The profile beyond {radius} is extrapolated. The quoted diameter is twice R₂₀₀ of the dark component alone, where its mean density is {overdensity} times critical density; it excludes baryons and is not a measured edge. Colour, central smoothing and the outer fade are illustration choices.

milkyway.title: Milky Way
milkyway.body: Our galaxy from outside, built on measurements: a thin and a thick disk, a peanut-shaped bulge inside a bar at {bar}°, four arms at a ~{pitch}° pitch placed where maser distances put them near the Sun, the short Local Arm just outside us, dust lanes on the arms' inner edges and the warp of the outer disk. The far side is extrapolated: the centre hides it from us. About {merger} billion years ago the Gaia-Enceladus merger stirred it and thickened its disk.
milkyway.caution: Spiral arms are not fixed structures: stars pass through them, whether the arms are long-lived density waves or come and go, which is still debated. The planets' plane is tilted by about {tilt}° to the Galaxy's, so the view turns as you pull out past the nearest stars.

proxima.where: Centaurus, near the southern Milky Way
proxima.motion: {velocity} km/s toward the Sun, {proper}″ a year across the sky
proxima.body: A red dwarf, the nearest star to the Sun. It is drawn where it really is on the sky; the ring is its distance and the beam links it to the Sun. The Sun's gravity is already losing to the Galaxy near the outer Oort cloud.

alphaCen.motion: {velocity} km/s toward the Sun; Proxima orbits the pair
alphaCen.body: Two Sun-like stars {distance} away, a close pair drawn as one point. Proxima is loosely bound to them, about {proxima} out. Both pass about {approach} from the Sun in roughly {years} years.

barnard.motion: {velocity} km/s toward the Sun, {proper}″ a year, the fastest proper motion known
barnard.body: A faint red dwarf {distance} away, closing fast. It passes about {approach} from the Sun in roughly {years} years, then recedes.

scholz.motion: {velocity} km/s away from the Sun, almost along the line of sight
scholz.body: A red dwarf with a brown-dwarf companion, receding. Run its track back and it passed through the outer Oort cloud about {flyby} thousand years ago, roughly a light-year out: the closest well-established stellar flyby. Humans were around and may have seen its flares.

stars.caution: Distances and directions are measured. Closest approaches follow straight-line tracks from measured speeds, good for a few hundred thousand years either way.

localGroup.title: Local Group
localGroup.members: About {value} galaxies, most of them dwarfs
localGroup.mass: A few trillion Suns, mostly dark matter
localGroup.body: Our galaxy's group: two giants, the Milky Way and Andromeda, with Triangulum and dozens of dwarfs, held together by their own gravity, so it does not expand with the Universe. By the timing argument the giants flew apart after the Big Bang, turned around about {turnaroundAgo} billion years ago at {turnaround}, and have been falling together since.
localGroup.caution: Only the named galaxies are at measured places; the dwarfs are a sketch around their hosts.

andromeda.title: Andromeda Galaxy
andromeda.approach: About {value} km/s toward the Milky Way ({sun} km/s toward the Sun)
andromeda.width: About {range}, from the bright disk to its faint outer edge
andromeda.future: A first close pass in ~{range} billion years is likely; a merger is possible, not certain
andromeda.body: The nearest big galaxy and the largest in the Local Group, a spiral like ours seen at a slant. Its spectrum shows it nearing the Sun at about {sun} km/s; take away the Sun's own orbit around the Galaxy and it closes on the Milky Way at about {approach} km/s. Gravity alone, that speed, today's {distance} and the age of the Universe fix one radial orbit: the timing argument.
andromeda.caution: Its sideways motion is uncertain, so studies put the chance of a merger within {within} billion years anywhere from about one half to nine in ten.

virgo.title: Virgo Cluster
virgo.heart: M87, with a black hole of about {value} Suns
virgo.body: The nearest large cluster and the heart of our supercluster. We are not inside it: the Local Group lies far out on the supercluster's outskirts, pulled toward the cluster while the expansion still carries us apart.
virgo.caution: The members are a drawn sample shaped like a cluster, not a catalogue.

supercluster.title: Virgo Supercluster
supercluster.body: Also called the Local Supercluster: a flattened spread of groups and clouds around Virgo, with the Local Group on one of its spurs. It is not bound, so it grows with the expansion; since 2014 it counts as one lobe of Laniakea.
supercluster.caution: Its clouds and spurs are a sketch; only the named groups and clusters are at measured places.

laniakea.title: Laniakea
laniakea.heart: The Great Attractor, ~{value} away toward Norma and Centaurus
laniakea.body: Laniakea was defined in 2014 as a basin of galaxy flows toward the Great Attractor, after subtracting cosmic expansion. Its historical marker remains here. The updated atlas also shows larger, probabilistic CF4 basins.
laniakea.caution: CF4 places the Milky Way in the Shapley basin in {shapley} of realizations and Ophiuchus in {ophiuchus}. This depends on reconstruction and smoothing. The optional flow lines are an illustration, not imported velocity data.

triangulum.title: Triangulum Galaxy
triangulum.future: May join the Milky Way–Andromeda merger
triangulum.body: The Local Group's third spiral, smaller and looser than ours, probably on a long orbit around Andromeda. Under a dark sky it is just visible to the eye, among the farthest things you can see without a telescope.
triangulum.caution: Whether it has already passed close to Andromeda is debated.

fornax.title: Fornax Cluster
fornax.body: After Virgo, the most massive cluster within about {within}, smaller and more compact, in the southern sky.
fornax.caution: The members are a drawn sample shaped like a cluster, not a catalogue.

centaurus.title: Centaurus Cluster
centaurus.body: A rich cluster on the run of galaxies from Virgo toward the Great Attractor, part of the Centaurus–Hydra concentration.
centaurus.caution: Its distance here comes from its redshift, not a direct measurement; the members are a drawn sample.

hydra.title: Hydra Cluster
hydra.body: A rich cluster at about the same distance as the Centaurus Cluster, part of the same concentration that feeds the Great Attractor.
hydra.caution: Its distance here comes from its redshift, not a direct measurement; the members are a drawn sample.

greatAttractor.title: Great Attractor
greatAttractor.where: Behind the Milky Way's disk, toward Norma and Centaurus
greatAttractor.body: Where Laniakea's flows converge: a concentration of clusters about {distance} away, mostly hidden by our own galaxy's dust and stars. Its pull showed up in galaxy motions in the 1980s before anyone could see what was there.
greatAttractor.caution: It is a region, not one object; its centre and mass differ between studies.

localSheet.title: Local Sheet
localSheet.members: The Local Group and a dozen nearby groups: M81, Centaurus A, Sculptor and more
localSheet.motion: Moving ~{value} km/s away from the Local Void; inside it, galaxies stray only ~{stray} km/s
localSheet.body: The thin wall of galaxies we live in: the Local Group and its neighbours lie in one flat slab about {radius} in radius. Its galaxies drift apart with the expansion almost in step, and the whole sheet is being pushed away from the emptiness of the Local Void beside it. It sits on the outskirts of the Virgo Supercluster.
localSheet.caution: Only the named groups are at measured places; the smaller groups in the sheet are a sketch.

perseusPisces.title: Perseus–Pisces Supercluster
perseusPisces.length: At least {value} along its main ridge
perseusPisces.where: Toward Perseus and Pisces, next door to Laniakea
perseusPisces.body: A long chain of galaxies and clusters, one of the clearest filaments in the nearby sky. It is a basin of its own beside Laniakea: galaxies on its side of the watershed flow toward it, not toward the Great Attractor.
perseusPisces.caution: The measured layer uses catalogue points. The optional illustrated chain follows a few measured cluster anchors; the Milky Way hides part of the region. Redshift distances retain peculiar-velocity distortions.

coma.title: Coma Cluster
coma.body: One of the richest clusters near us. In 1933 Fritz Zwicky found its galaxies moving far too fast to be held by the matter that shines: an early strong hint of dark matter.
coma.caution: Its distance here comes from its redshift, which the cluster’s own motion can shift by a few per cent; the members are a drawn sample.

shapley.title: Shapley Supercluster
shapley.members: {clusters} clusters in its velocity range; about {galaxies} galaxies measured in its field
shapley.where: Far beyond the Centaurus Cluster, in the same part of the sky
shapley.body: One of the largest concentrations of matter in the nearby universe. With the Great Attractor it pulls on the Local Group, though how much of our motion it explains is still debated.
shapley.caution: Mass depends on the region and reconstruction. The observed CLASSIX members, the supercluster’s historical marker and the larger Shapley flow basin have separate meanings.

sloanGreatWall.title: Sloan Great Wall
sloanGreatWall.length: About {value}; {past} when the light we see left it
sloanGreatWall.where: Along the celestial equator, from Hydra through Sextans and Leo to Virgo
sloanGreatWall.body: A wall of galaxy clusters about {distance} away, found in 2003 in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey’s map. We see it as it was when its light left; the map places it where it is now, stretched with the expansion since.
sloanGreatWall.caution: A galaxy wall and its larger flow basin are different structures. The old illustrated outline is optional; the 2026 Sloan-basin interpretation has its own preprint card.

observableUniverse.title: Observable universe
observableUniverse.cmb: From {distance}, set out {age} thousand years after the Big Bang
observableUniverse.age: {value} billion years of light on its way
observableUniverse.body: Everything we could ever have seen. Light has had {age} billion years to reach us, but space kept stretching while it travelled, so its sources now lie much farther away. Its farthest visible light is the cosmic microwave background, from when the universe first turned transparent: a limit on what light can show, not an edge. We sit at the centre only because every observer sits at the centre of their own.
observableUniverse.caution: The rings mark where light set out {near}, {mid} and {far} billion years ago, at today’s model-derived distances. The CMB uses foreground-cleaned Planck and optional ACT data; its spherical placement is illustrative. Generated galaxies beyond the web appear only in Illustration and Both modes. Dark or empty areas do not imply a measured absence of radiation or matter.

quipu.body: The bright points are the observed CLASSIX member clusters, with sky positions and spectroscopic redshifts. Their collective structure was identified by a friends-of-friends analysis. The label sits at their unweighted spatial centroid; the total mass is inferred.
quipu.caution: The published extent uses H₀ = {hubble}. The map converts redshifts using its Planck cosmology. Membership does not establish that the whole structure is gravitationally bound.

vela.body: The updated CF4++ZOA reconstruction includes galaxies obscured by the Milky Way. The diamond marks the reconstructed density peak. The dashed circle gives the radius of a sphere with the same total overdense volume.
vela.caution: Accepted by A&A; values from manuscript v2. The circle is a size guide, not the structure’s shape. The published mass uses H₀ = {hubble} and a different region from the collapsing knots catalogue.

southPoleWall.body: A wall inferred from galaxy motions in Cosmicflows-3. The diamond marks its approximate density peak at the celestial south pole, named Chamaeleon+11.8 in the paper.
southPoleWall.caution: This marker locates a published reconstruction. It does not trace the wall’s surface; no artificial bridge joins gaps in the observations. The newer basin catalogue describes a different, flow-defined region.

shapleyBasin.body: Cosmicflows-4 reconstructs a large basin of galaxy flows around Shapley. The cross spans the published positional spread along the supergalactic axes. The supercluster’s observed concentration and its larger flow basin are separate objects.
shapleyBasin.caution: The Milky Way membership fraction counts reconstruction realizations whose flow ends in this basin. It is distinct from the probability that the basin exists, and does not define a bound edge.

sloanBasin.body: The 2026 Sloan-basin preprint interprets the larger flow domain around the Sloan Great Wall. Its centre and existence probability here come from the published 2024 CF4 basin catalogue.
sloanBasin.caution: Preprint interpretation. The southern extent is limited by survey coverage and remains open. The effective radius summarizes a catalogue volume; no closed basin boundary is drawn.

ophiuchusBasin.body: This CF4 flow basin is one possible home for the Milky Way, near the region traditionally called Laniakea. Other reconstruction realizations place our flow in the larger Shapley basin.
ophiuchusBasin.caution: Flow basins depend on the data, smoothing scale and model. The displayed membership and basin-existence probabilities answer different questions; neither is a measured border.

localVoid.body: The Local Void entry in the 2026 CF4++ZOA V-web catalogue. The dashed circles compare effective radii of the full reconstructed region and its more persistent subvolume.
localVoid.caution: Preprint. The inner guide represents volume classified as void in at least {support} of realizations. The circles are size guides, not physical surfaces or radial error bars.

northernLocalVoid.body: The Northern Local Void entry in the 2026 CF4++ZOA V-web catalogue. Its centre is taken from the published supergalactic Cartesian coordinates.
northernLocalVoid.caution: Preprint. The inner guide represents volume classified as void in at least {support} of realizations. The circles are size guides, not physical surfaces or radial error bars.

sculptorVoid.body: The Sculptor Void entry in the 2026 CF4++ZOA V-web catalogue. A reconstructed underdensity is different from a blank patch in an incomplete galaxy survey.
sculptorVoid.caution: Preprint. The inner guide represents volume classified as void in at least {support} of realizations. The circles are size guides, not physical surfaces or radial error bars.

cosmicSurveys.body: Points use measured sky coordinates and redshifts from Cosmicflows-4 groups, CLASSIX clusters and a sparse sample of DESI DR1 galaxies. Radial positions are derived with the map’s Planck cosmology. The smaller render-quality settings draw fewer records without moving them.
cosmicSurveys.caution: These are overlapping, incomplete surveys with different selection functions. Point brightness is illustrative. Missing points are not evidence of a void. Nearby negative redshifts cannot give a Hubble-flow distance and are omitted from this layer; the local maps cover that regime.

cosmicBasins.body: All entries from the published CF4 basin catalogue are drawn as crosses at their inferred centres. Each arm spans one standard deviation along a supergalactic coordinate axis. Vela and the South Pole Wall have separate peak markers.
cosmicBasins.caution: These are summaries of reconstructions, not measured velocity arrows or complete basin surfaces. Some candidate basins appear in only a minority of posterior realizations. The Sloan interpretation has a separately labelled preprint card.

cosmicVoids.body: The complete void table from the 2026 CF4++ZOA V-web preprint. Dashed outer circles represent effective radii; inner circles represent the more persistent subvolumes. The named voids can be opened individually in the finder.
cosmicVoids.caution: Preprint, using the authors’ zero eigenvalue threshold. Changing that threshold changes the catalogue. A circle carries the same volume as the region, but does not reproduce its shape; the inner guide is not a confidence interval on radius.

cosmicKnots.body: The complete knot table from the 2026 CF4++ZOA V-web preprint. Small wire diamonds mark regions where the reconstructed velocity field contracts along every principal axis.
cosmicKnots.caution: Preprint. Diamond sizes are symbols, not measured cluster radii. These dynamical regions differ from galaxy clusters, full overdense superclusters, and flow basins, so their masses and boundaries must not be interchanged.

solar.scatteredWhere: Near Neptune at closest, hundreds of au out at farthest
solar.sun: Our star. Seen from Alpha Centauri it would be one more bright point in Cassiopeia.
solar.mercury: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. From Earth it never strays far from the Sun, so it shows only near dawn or dusk.
solar.venus: Clouds of sulphuric acid over a crushing carbon-dioxide air; the brightest planet in our sky.
solar.earth: Home, and where Deep Field looks out from: every 'light left' counts back from now.
solar.mars: A cold, dusty desert with the tallest volcano known, Olympus Mons.
solar.jupiter: The largest planet, more than twice as massive as all the others together.
solar.saturn: A gas giant less dense than water, circled by rings of bright ice.
solar.uranus: An ice giant tipped on its side, so each pole gets decades of daylight, then decades of night.
solar.neptune: The outermost planet, found in 1846 where mathematics said it had to be.
solar.pluto: A dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt. New Horizons flew past in 2015 and found a vast plain of nitrogen ice.
solar.sedna: A distant, reddish world found in 2003, on an orbit that never comes near the planets.
solar.halley: The best-known comet: last near the Sun in 1986, back in 2061.
solar.asteroids: Millions of rocky bodies between Mars and Jupiter, yet all together a small fraction of the Moon's mass: the belt is mostly empty space.
solar.kuiper: A broad ring of icy bodies beyond Neptune, Pluto among them; many short-period comets start out here.
solar.scattered: Icy bodies on long, tilted orbits that Neptune's gravity flung outward.
solar.oort: A vast shell of icy bodies, inferred from long-period comets and never seen directly. Its outer edge reaches perhaps halfway to the nearest stars.
solar.tracer: One sample of the population, on a realistic orbit. It is not a real catalogued object.

reach.predicted: Earth no longer hears it: its place is predicted from its last tracking.
reach.shape: Two crossings are all we have measured, so its shape is unknown; it is drawn here as a sphere.
reach.heliopause: Where the Sun's wind stops against the thin gas between the stars. Past it lies interstellar space.
reach.voyager1: Flew past Jupiter and Saturn, then kept going. In 2012 it became the first craft in interstellar space, and it is the farthest we have reached.
reach.voyager2: The only craft to visit Uranus and Neptune. It crossed into interstellar space in 2018, far to the south of where Voyager 1 crossed.
reach.pioneer10: The first craft through the asteroid belt and the first to Jupiter, in 1973. Its last faint signal reached Earth in 2003.
reach.pioneer11: The first to Saturn, in 1979, after Jupiter. It went silent in 1995.
reach.newHorizons: Flew past Pluto in 2015 and Arrokoth in 2019, the farthest world any craft has visited.

technicalDetails.title: Inside Deep Field
technicalDetails.summary: Today's sky at every scale: the nearest stars from Gaia astrometry, a Milky Way built on measurements where they exist, named galaxies and clusters at their measured places, and flat ΛCDM for distances and light-travel times. The sources below separate measured quantities from sketches.

features.views: Fifteen views from the inner planets to the observable universe, on one zoom.
features.depth: A depth ladder and an eyepiece: how far a place is, when its light left and its redshift.
features.objects: The Sun and planets, the nearest stars and Scholz's star, the Milky Way's structure, the Local Group, the Virgo Cluster, Laniakea, the cosmic web and the microwave background, each with a card that says what is measured.

solar.title: The solar system today
solar.body: The planets, Pluto, Sedna and Halley's comet sit where JPL's orbital elements put them on today's date, with the Moon and the large moons of the giants. The asteroid belt, the Kuiper belt and the Oort cloud are samples drawn to their measured or inferred extents, not catalogues. It is the Orrery's solar system held at today; the Orrery shows how it got there.

stars.title: The Sun's neighbourhood
stars.body: The nearest stars sit at their Gaia DR3 positions and parallaxes (α Centauri's from ALMA, Scholz's star's from Dupuy et al. 2019). Their closest approaches come from straight-line tracks through measured proper motions and radial velocities, good for a few hundred thousand years; Scholz's star's flyby through the outer Oort cloud falls out of that. Behind them the bright stars of the shared J2000 catalogue sit in their real directions, and the Milky Way band is the Galaxy map itself, seen from the Sun.

galaxy.title: The Sun's galactic orbit
galaxy.body: The Sun circles {sunRadiusKpc} kpc from the centre (GRAVITY) with a {galacticYearMyr}-million-year period, clockwise from the north galactic pole. Today it sits near the inner end of a ~{radialSwingKpc} kpc radial swing (period ~{radialMyr} Myr) and {heightPc} pc north of the plane, climbing through ±{verticalPc} pc (period ~{verticalMyr} Myr). The gold line runs those oscillations back over two laps; the true phase that long ago is unknown. The disk follows measured structure: exponential thin ({thinLengthKpc} kpc, {thinHeightPc} pc) and thick ({thickLengthKpc} kpc, {thickHeightPc} pc) disks, a boxy bulge inside a {barHalfKpc} kpc half-length bar at {barDeg}°, four logarithmic arms at a {pitchDeg}° pitch anchored to maser parallaxes near the Sun, the Local Arm, dust on the arms' inner edges and the Cepheid-traced warp beyond {warpStartKpc} kpc. The halo projects a spherical NFW model derived from Feng et al. (2026). Its optional density guide marks R₂₀₀ ≈ {haloKpc} kpc for the dark component alone; the outer profile is extrapolated. The far side of the disk is extrapolated.

cosmos.title: Beyond the Milky Way
cosmos.body: Named nearby galaxies retain their measured anchors, including Andromeda ({andromedaMly} million light-years, approaching at {andromedaKms} km/s). Beyond them, the atlas imports {cf4Groups} {cf4GroupsPlural, select, one {CF4 group record} other {CF4 group records}}, {classixClusters} {classixClustersPlural, select, one {CLASSIX cluster} other {CLASSIX clusters}} and {desiGalaxies} {desiGalaxiesPlural, select, one {sampled DESI DR1 galaxy} other {sampled DESI DR1 galaxies}}. Sky positions and redshifts are measured; radial distances use flat ΛCDM (H₀ = {hubble} km/s/Mpc, Ωm = {omegaM}). CF4 redshifts already use the CMB frame. Observer-frame CLASSIX and DESI redshifts receive the dipole correction; peculiar velocities remain. The sparse DESI sample is not a complete survey or coverage mask. Hollow markers locate {basinCount} {basinCountPlural, select, one {published CF4 basin centre} other {published CF4 basin centres}} with coordinate-spread crosses available on inspection. Vela uses the accepted 2026 v2 reconstruction; the South Pole Wall has an approximate peak marker. The {voidCount} {voidCountPlural, select, one {void} other {voids}} and {knotCount} {knotCountPlural, select, one {knot} other {knots}} come from explicitly labelled 2026 preprint tables. Supergalactic coordinates in h⁻¹ Mpc use h = {atlasH}. Void circles and the Vela circle are equivalent-volume size guides, not surfaces. The inner void circles describe subvolumes persistent in {voidSupport}% of realizations, not radial uncertainties. The older seeded web and flow paths remain a separate illustration. Data, Illustration and Both modes control the overlay; Both preserves the familiar Laniakea shape alongside the catalogues. Local galaxy populations remain illustrations. Generated galaxies beyond the web are hidden in Data mode. The CMB uses masked Planck 2018 SMICA temperatures with optional ACT DR6.02 NILC detail inside its trusted footprint; neither data gaps nor load failures are filled with synthetic CMB. Foreground-cleaned temperatures are reconstructions; sphere placement, colour and opacity are illustrative. The observable-universe horizon and microwave background follow the same cosmology, including radiation; its age is {universeGyr} billion years.

depth.title: Distance and light
depth.body: The ladder is the camera's distance on a log scale, from the Sun's neighbourhood to past the microwave background. The eyepiece reads how far the view reaches (its centre's distance from the Sun plus half the field), or the distance of the selected object. Up to a million light-years the light's travel time in years is its distance in light-years. Farther, the redshift is the one whose comoving distance matches, found by inverting the ΛCDM distance integral (the cosmological redshift alone: a galaxy's own motion shifts its measured one a little), and the light left at that redshift's lookback time. Nothing beyond the microwave background can be seen, so the readout stops there.

sunlight.title: Light takes time
sunlight.body: Even sunlight is old: it left the Sun minutes before it reaches us. The rulers give each planet's distance from Earth and how long its light takes.

giants.title: Hours away
giants.body: Past the giant planets, light needs hours. The line below says how long ago the light at the edge of the view set out.

voyager.title: Our farthest reach
voyager.body: Five probes are leaving the Sun. The farthest, Voyager 1, entered interstellar space in 2012; its signal now takes about a day to reach us.

oort.title: The Sun's last outpost
oort.body: The Oort cloud of icy comets reaches perhaps halfway to the nearest stars. Nobody has seen it directly.

stars.title: Years of light
stars.body: Proxima's light set out over four years ago. Every star we see shows its past, not its present.

galaxy.title: One star among billions
galaxy.body: The Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way's disk. Light from the Galaxy's far side left during the last ice age.

andromeda.title: Our big neighbour
andromeda.body: Andromeda's light left when early humans were already shaping stone tools. The gap is closing: billions of years from now the two galaxies will probably pass close, and may merge.

virgo.title: A city of galaxies
virgo.body: More than a thousand galaxies, whose pull reaches all the way to us. This light set out not long after the dinosaurs died out.

laniakea.title: Our home basin
laniakea.body: Galaxies stream toward the Great Attractor like rivers toward the sea. This basin of flows is our supercluster, Laniakea.

web.title: The cosmic web
web.body: On the largest scales, galaxies line walls and filaments around vast, nearly empty voids. The inset shows a separate observed survey field: mass reconstructed from Webb galaxy shapes, not the local web’s three-dimensional density.

firstLight.title: The oldest light
firstLight.body: Farther means earlier. Beyond the farthest galaxies seen lie cosmic dawn and the dark ages, and behind them glows the oldest light we see, set free soon after the Big Bang. Explore how the assumed cosmology changes separations below; the diagram is a model, not a movie of these galaxies.

darkHalo.title: The mass we infer
darkHalo.body: Stellar motions reveal more gravity than ordinary matter supplies. This pale overlay is one inferred dark-matter density model. Its outer regions are extrapolated; there is no sharp shell.

modeHints.data: Large-scale catalogue points and labelled reconstructions. No illustrated web or flow paths. Your data-layer filters are remembered when you switch modes.
modeHints.illustration: The illustrated cosmic web and familiar Laniakea flow shape. These paths convey structure; they are not imported galaxy velocities or measured boundaries.
modeHints.both: Catalogue data and reconstructed centres alongside the illustrated web and Laniakea flow paths. Filled points, hollow markers and illustrated paths retain their separate meanings.

atlas.experienceModes: Drift uses Illustration; Guide uses Both. Both hide the full uncertainty overlay and restore your manual settings when they end. The CMB uses observational maps in every mode.
atlas.guideMode: Both: measured points, reconstructed centres and illustrated flows.
atlas.coverage: Measured angles and redshifts give model-dependent distances. The surveys overlap and leave gaps; a blank patch is not a detected void. Lower render quality subsamples the measured records.
atlas.glyphs: Small hollow rings mark reconstructed centres; flat diamonds mark inferred knots. Selecting a structure reveals its positional uncertainty bars or dashed size circles. These guides describe uncertainty or equivalent volume, not physical boundaries. Enable all guides to compare them across the map. Voids, knots and the newer Sloan interpretation are labelled preprints.

sources.brooks2026: Brooks et al. · 2026 · outer halo & LMC

halo.body: A pale density overlay shows one spherical dark-matter model around the Milky Way. Its colour and opacity make invisible mass legible; they do not represent light.
halo.measured: Gaia measures stellar positions, proper motions and radial velocities. Cepheid distances and a rotation curve constrain the gravitational field; dark-matter density is inferred after accounting for ordinary matter.
halo.inferred: This NFW illustration matches the rounded mean density and enclosed dark mass in Feng et al. (2026), choosing the extended scale-radius solution. It is not a unique fit or a measured shape. The outer halo is extrapolated; baryonic assumptions and the LMC affect mass estimates. No full uncertainty band is claimed.
halo.alt: Dark-matter density of the halo model against distance from the Galaxy's centre, both logarithmic: solid where stellar motions constrain it, dashed where it is extrapolated, with the Sun and the density radius marked.
halo.axes: Distance from the centre · density, both logarithmic. Dashed: extrapolated.

lensing.alt: COSMOS-Web projected E-mode convergence map reconstructed from galaxy shape distortions, with the unsurveyed exterior masked.
lensing.legend: Blue: negative κ · gold: positive κ. Nonlinear contrast. Blank exterior: no map coverage.
lensing.note: The published COSMOS-Web map reconstructs projected total mass, including ordinary matter, from weak lensing. It has no assigned three-dimensional depth. Negative convergence means a relative mass deficit, not negative mass. Edge structure and small features are affected by noise and reconstruction.
lensing.measured: Webb measures images of background galaxies. Their small shape distortions are combined statistically to infer the lensing field. These coloured pixels are a mass reconstruction, not a photograph of dark matter.

expansion.alt: Calculated cosmic scale factor versus cosmic age in the Planck flat Lambda-CDM model, with a movable epoch marker.
expansion.axes: Horizontal: cosmic age · vertical: relative separation a(t)
expansion.note: This curve uses the same flat ΛCDM model as the atlas. Dark energy has constant density; its fraction grows as matter dilutes. Separations refer to the homogeneous cosmic background. Bound galaxies do not expand with this diagram, and the camera’s lookback view is unchanged.
expansion.measured: DESI measures spectra and redshifts. Its correlation analysis infers transverse and radial distances relative to the sound horizon r_d. The latest checked anchor is shown below; it does not independently measure dark energy or replace the baseline curve.
expansion.provisional: DESI DR2 IV (August 2026 version) is a preprint at our review. Its combinations of data still favour evolving dark energy to different degrees; this is not an established discovery. The quoted errors are correlated marginal uncertainties.

cmb.title: Cosmic microwave background
cmb.open: Open CMB data sources, colour scale and reconstruction limits
cmb.maskLegend: Dark patches are masked, not colder
cmb.measured: Planck and ACT measured microwave sky brightness. The colours show temperature differences in the CMB signal, not galaxies or visible light.
cmb.processing: Foreground removal reconstructs that signal from several frequencies. ACT detail uses the released ACT–Planck combination with thermal SZ deprojected; residual foregrounds and noise remain.
cmb.colours: Temperature difference: blue −{limit} µK · grey zero · amber +{limit} µK. Values beyond the ends saturate. Dark patches are masked, not colder.
cmb.geometry: The sky directions are Galactic coordinates centred on our observer. Wrapping them on a sphere at the model’s last-scattering distance is an illustration, not a measured three-dimensional surface or an edge of space. Only the facing hemisphere is drawn.
cmb.masks: Planck confidence and inpainting masks exclude unreliable or filled-in pixels. ACT detail is restricted to its trusted footprint and excludes inpainted sources. Elsewhere, valid Planck data is used; where neither is valid the map stays masked.
cmb.resolution: Both maps are downsampled for display: longitude spacing is {planck} for Planck and {act} for ACT. This is not native telescope resolution. The colour scale and opacity are display choices.
cmb.releases: The all-sky baseline is the released Planck 2018 SMICA product, not the newer PR4 frequency maps. ACT detail uses DR6.02. These are pinned products, not a live feed.
cmb.modeNote: All modes use the same observational CMB reconstruction. Data mode hides the generated distant galaxies. ACT detail applies only within its valid footprint.

status.unavailable: Planck unavailable · no all-sky CMB map
